newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine VP wants hi-tech "detente" to save jobs.
newsitem.headline: Argentine VP wants hi-tech "detente" to save jobs.

text.p: Argentine Vice-President Carlos Ruckauf Monday urged an international "detente" on the use of high technology in the workplace to combat growing unemployment, which stands at over 17 percent in Argentina.
"Just like at one time there was talk of nuclear detente, some time we will have to consider a high-technology detente to stop technology replacing man," Ruckauf told foreign correspondents.
The Peronist government official said such an agreement in the context of the International Labour Organization or United Nations, was the only way to combat "structural unemployment."
Argentina's stubbornly high jobless rate is the biggest headache of President Carlos Menem's ruling Peronists in the run-up to mid-term elections in Congress in October.

Opinion polls consistently show job security is the main concern of the Argentine people. One survey published Monday in La Nacion newspaper, showed 60 percent of those surveyed in Buenos Aires consider it Argentina's biggest problem.

Trade unions, the opposition and some Peronist dissidents put the blame on the free-market economic reforms that Menem has implemented since coming to power in 1989, shedding his party's traditional alliance with the labor movement.

Ruckauf, who calls himself a "Peronist" rather than a "Menemist" and is closer in ideology to Buenos Aires Provincial Governor Eduardo Duhalde, the leading contender so far to succeed Menem in 1999, than to Menem.
Gov. Duhalde is an old-fashioned Peronist whose answer to unemployment is labor-intensive public works projects, such as road-mending gangs equipped solely with pick and shovel.

Ruckauf made it clear that he does not blame free-market reforms for Argentina's high jobless rate: "I don't think this is happening simply because the market has taken the place of the state...but because of excess technology."
He said businessmen who believe in "extreme capitalism" should ask themselves the following question: "If the world keeps losing jobs, who are the consumers going to be?"
